implementation_notes: C has no reflection and cannot define a type at run time, so the proxy is a struct pairing a target pointer with a const table of function pointers, and every proxied operation must be declared where the compiler can see it. The only way to fabricate callable entries at run time is libffi's closure API: ffi_closure_alloc() reserves a writable block and returns an executable code pointer which ffi_prep_closure_loc() fills with a trampoline that reifies its arguments into void** and calls the handler - the mechanism GLib/GObject uses for signal marshalling (g_cclosure_marshal_generic). Use it when the interface set comes from a foreign runtime (scripting engine, IPC binding); otherwise a static table is simpler and never touches executable memory.
pitfalls: ffi_prep_closure_loc writes executable code: on W^X-hardened systems the allocation can fail, and the ffi_cif plus every ffi_type it points at must outlive the closure or the trampoline reads freed descriptors.

Closures are heap state: ffi_closure_free() must run exactly once, and a proxy struct that merely stores the target pointer does not participate in ownership, so the target can be freed while the proxy is still reachable.
There is no discovery of the wrapped interface: adding a method to the vtable silently leaves generated call sites forwarding through the old table.

variants.name: hand-written const function-pointer table
variants.idiom_name: const struct of function pointers delegating to the target
variants.implementation_notes: The classic realization without runtime generation: a const struct of function pointers is the interface, and each behaviour supplies its own table while the proxy stores the target. Interception is uniform only because that table is the single dispatch point, and adding a method means editing the table and every implementation - which is why IDL-driven or generated tables dominate real C codebases.
pitfalls: Every implementation must fill every slot: a missing handler is a null call at run time, not a compile error, because C cannot require completeness of a table.
Erasing the target to void* loses const and ownership intent; a proxy that returns borrowed data from a target it does not own is a use-after-free waiting to happen.
